newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK C.BANKER SAYS NO NEED FOR DEVALUATION.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK C.BANKER SAYS NO NEED FOR DEVALUATION.

text.p: The National Bank of Slovakia said on Tuesday there was no need to devalue the Slovak crown and that the currency's current level was suitable at present.

"I only repeat what has been previously stated --we see no reason for devaluation at present and we will continue to use the current fluctuation band more intensively," Frantisek Szulenyi, NBS Treasury Director, told Reuters.
The NBS fixes the crown daily against a 60/40 percent mark/dollar basket within plus/minus seven percent of the basket's midpoint calculated at 1130 CET (0930 GMT).

On Tuesday the NBS continued to match the market fixing the crown at 33.359 to the dollar and 19.554 to the mark, implying a depreciation against the midpoint of -0.76 percent, after fixing it at -0.73 percent on Monday.
"As we are currently keeping the crown at parity, it is probably a suitable level (at present)," Szulenyi said.
"I cannot say where (which side of the band) we shall keep...it will depend on the situation at the central bank fixing and the country's balance of payments," he added.

The NBS has been fixing the crown between its basket midpoint and the -1.0 percent level of its band for nearly a month, and has been fixing it roughly within a three percent range around the midpoint level for over a year.
Slovakia's burgeoning current account deficit of $1.94 billion in 1996, largely propped up by short-term capital inflows, has prompted renewed analyst concerns of a possible devaluation of the crown.
But Szulenyi said the Slovak banking sector was currently "stabilised and balanced", with banks still tending to be short.
He added that "nothing extraordinary" had happened in foreign exchange trading at the NBS's fixing for the past two weeks.

The devaluation concerns have risen also due to the recent depreciation of the Czech crown. The Czech Republic split with former federation partner Slovakia in 1993 but the two remain each other's largest trading partner.
"We have been watching the Czech crown developments, but it is no guideline for us," Szulenyi said.
He said the NBS's foreign exchange reserves were stable, but added that "views vary of whether they are at the optimum or minimum level".
